title: Colcannon
subtitle: Irish mashed potato with kale and spring onion
excerpt: Floury potatoes mashed with melted butter, warm milk, shredded kale, and spring onion. Served with a well of butter melting in the centre. The finest version of mashed potato there is.

recipe.sourceNotes: Colcannon is a traditional Irish dish of mashed potato combined with kale or cabbage, recorded in Irish literature since the 18th century. The name comes from the Irish 'cal ceannann', meaning white-headed cabbage. It is associated with Halloween in Ireland, where coins and thimbles were traditionally hidden inside it as charms. The distinguishing feature is the spring onion (scallion in Irish usage), which is warmed in the butter and milk before being incorporated into the mash, and the well of extra butter in the centre that melts as the dish is served.

content.text: Use the floury potatoes: waxy potatoes will give a gluey result when mashed. Steam or boil them in their skins if possible, then peel after cooking: the mash will be drier and fluffier. Do not over-mash or the starch will break down and the potato will become sticky. The kale needs only a brief blanch: it should still have some body in the finished dish.
Boil the potatoes in well-salted water until completely tender, about 20 minutes. Drain and leave to steam-dry for 5 minutes.
Blanch the kale in boiling salted water for 2 minutes. Drain well and squeeze out the excess water.
Warm the butter and milk together in a small pan over low heat. Add the spring onion and heat for 1 minute until softened slightly.
Mash the potatoes until smooth. Beat in the buttery milk and spring onion mixture. Fold in the kale. Season generously. Serve in a mound with a large knob of butter pressed into the centre.
